q: In AM (amplitude modulation), which property of the carrier is varied?
why: AM varies the carrier's height to carry the data; FM varies frequency, PM varies phase.

q: In a quantizer, the set of input-interval boundaries that map to the same output level is the:
why: Boundaries form the coder mapping; the representative output values form the decoder mapping.

q: What are the three stages of every compression scheme, in order?
why: Transform to an easier representation, introduce loss (quantization), then assign codewords.

q: Which stage is the main lossy step in compression?
why: Quantization uses fewer reconstruction levels than the original, so information is necessarily lost.

q: How is the compression ratio defined?
choices: B0 − B1 (the number of bits saved)
why: Compression ratio = B0/B1, and a good codec has a ratio much larger than 1.

q: Self-information log2(1/p_i) corresponds to:
choices: The bits needed to encode symbol s_i
The probability of the symbol s_i
The average code length of the whole code
why: Shannon's self-information is the ideal number of bits for that symbol.

q: Entropy of an image whose 256 grey levels are all equally likely?
The two-valued image on slide 13 has entropy about:
why: With p = 1/3 and 2/3, η ≈ 0.918 ≈ 0.92, under 1 bit.

q: Entropy of a source with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8?
Self-information of a symbol with p = 1/8?
why: log2(1/(1/8)) = log2 8 = 3. (0.375 is p·log2(1/p), its contribution to η.)

q: Entropy of the string HELLO, roughly?
why: 0.4·1.32 + 3·0.2·2.32 ≈ 1.922. 2.0 is the Huffman average, not η.

q: For HELLO the slide's 'log2' column shows 1.32 for L. What is it?
choices: The code length given to L
The entropy of the whole string
why: log2(5/2) = 1.32 is L's self-information, not its actual code length (1 bit).

q: Which value can the entropy of an n-symbol source NOT exceed?
why: η ≤ log2 n, with equality only for a uniform distribution.

q: A memoryless source is one where:
choices: Each symbol is independent of earlier ones
Symbols always come in long runs
The dictionary is rebuilt for every symbol
Every symbol has exactly the same probability
why: Memoryless = independently distributed; the current symbol does not depend on previous ones.

q: Run-length coding exploits:
why: RLC encodes a symbol plus the length of its continuous group.

q: RLC of BBBBEEEEEEEECCCCDAAAAA?
why: Runs are 4 B, 8 E, 4 C, 1 D, 5 A, written count-then-symbol.

q: 22 characters RLC-encode to 4B8E4C1D5A. Ratio in characters?
RLC-encoding ABCABC (count + symbol) gives how many characters?
why: 1A1B1C1A1B1C, twice the input: RLC expands data without runs.

q: Shannon-Fano coding is a:
why: It sorts symbols and recursively splits them into halves of equal count.

q: After sorting by count, Shannon-Fano repeatedly:
choices: Splits the list into two near-equal-count parts
Merges the two lowest-count symbols together
Adds the current string to a dictionary
Narrows an interval inside [0, 1) after each symbol
why: Recursive division into two parts of about equal total count until each part has one symbol.

q: Why does the slide show two Shannon-Fano trees for HELLO?
choices: The splits are not unique; both are valid
The second tree fixes an error in the first
One is Shannon-Fano and the other Huffman
One tree is the encoder's, one the decoder's
why: Different equally balanced splits are legal; here both give 10 bits.

q: Counts A15 B7 C6 D6 E5: Shannon-Fano needs 89 bits. Huffman needs:
why: Huffman gives A 1 bit and the rest 3 bits: 15 + 24·3 = 87, beating Shannon-Fano.

q: Each Huffman step combines:
choices: The first and the last symbols
Any two adjacent entries in the list
why: Pick the two smallest (leaf or parent), make them siblings under a parent with the summed probability.

q: Must the leaves be sorted before building a Huffman tree?
why: Slide 25: leaves can be sorted, 'though this is not necessary'.

q: Fixed-length code for 6 distinct symbols needs how many bits each?
why: ⌈log2 6⌉ = 3: bits must be whole.

q: Huffman codes L=0, H=10, E=110, O=111 for HELLO. Average code length?
why: 10 bits / 5 symbols = 2.0.

q: Slide 29: after iteration (a) the list is L P1 H. Which symbols formed P1?
why: P1 merges the two count-1 symbols E and O; H stays in the list.

q: Huffman for a: 1/2, b: 1/4, c: 1/8, d: 1/8. Average length?
why: Lengths 1,2,3,3 → 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.375 + 0.375 = 1.75, exactly the entropy.

q: MISSISSIPPI (I4 S4 P2 M1) Huffman-coded takes how many bits?
why: Lengths 1 and 2 for S and I, 3 for P and M: 4+8+6+3 = 21 (fixed 2-bit = 22).

q: SHAHZODA (H2 A2, S Z O D 1 each) Huffman-coded takes:
why: H, A get 2 bits, the four singles 3 bits: 8 + 12 = 20 (2.5 bits/letter = η).

q: Code lengths 1,2,3,4,4 for p = .4,.2,.2,.1,.1. Average length?
why: .4 + .4 + .6 + .4 + .4 = 2.2. A tree with lengths 2,2,2,3,3 also gives 2.2.

q: Two students build different Huffman trees for the same source (ties broken differently). Then:
choices: Both are optimal, with equal average length
Only the one with sorted leaves is correct
The one with the shorter longest code wins
Their codes give different compression ratios
why: Tie-breaking changes codes and even code lengths, but the average length is the same minimum.

q: The unique prefix property means:
choices: No codeword is a prefix of another
Every codeword starts with the same bit
Every codeword has exactly the same length
Codewords are sorted by their prefix
why: It precludes ambiguity in decoding, so no separators are needed.

q: In an optimal Huffman code, the two least frequent symbols:
choices: Have equal length, differing in the last bit
Get the two shortest codewords in the code
Always get the codes 0 and 1 respectively
Differ from each other in their very first bit
why: They are siblings at the deepest level, so same length, last bit differs.

q: Huffman's average code length L̄ satisfies:
why: Eq. 7.6: within one bit of the entropy, never below it.

q: A source has η = 2.3 bits. Which Huffman average length is impossible?
why: L̄ must lie in [2.3, 3.3); 3.4 is outside the bound.

q: Is the code a=0, b=01, c=10 uniquely decodable?
choices: Yes: all its codewords are different
Yes: it has fewer than four symbols
No: c is longer than both a and b
why: 0 is a prefix of 01, so the bitstream is ambiguous.

q: Efficiency of a code with η = 1.922 and L̄ = 2.0?
Why is plain Huffman wasteful when one p_i is very large?
choices: Codes must be whole bits, at least 1
It cannot code more than 2 symbols
The tree grows deeper than log2 n
The prefix property no longer holds for it
why: The ideal length log2(1/p_i) is near 0, but Huffman still spends at least 1 bit.

q: p(A)=0.9, p(B)=0.1, Huffman on pairs gives 1.29 bits per pair. Bits per symbol?
What does the slide say about extended Huffman's gain?
choices: It is worse than plain Huffman
It removes the need for a tree
why: Better than plain Huffman but modest, and n^k tables get huge for k ≥ 3.

q: For adaptive Huffman to decode correctly, the encoder and decoder must:
choices: Use the same initial_code and update_tree
Exchange the whole tree after every symbol
Use different trees for odd and even symbols
Agree only on the final frequency counts
why: If the routines differ, the trees diverge and decoding fails.

q: When a swap is needed, which node is swapped with the node just incremented to N+1?
choices: The farthest node with count N
The nearest node with count N+1
The root node of the whole tree
The leaf with the smallest count
why: Swap rule: the farthest node with count N is swapped with the node whose count became N+1.

q: LZW uses:
choices: Variable-length codes for each single symbol
One real number for the whole of the input message
why: Fixed-length codewords represent variable-length strings that occur together.

q: How does the LZW decoder get the dictionary?
choices: It rebuilds it dynamically from the codes
The encoder sends it before the data
It is fixed by the standard in advance, like ASCII
It is stored at the end of the file
why: Encoder and decoder build the same dictionary as the data flows.

q: Which is NOT an advantage of LZW over Huffman listed on the slide?
choices: It is lossy, so it gets higher ratios
No prior knowledge of the data needed
It compresses the data in a single pass
Better on files with repetitive data
why: LZW is lossless; the other three are listed advantages (plus 60–70% on some text).

q: In LZW compression, if s + c is already in the dictionary:
choices: Set s = s + c; output nothing
Add s + c again with a new code
why: Only extend the current string; output and add happen when s + c is new.

q: LZW of ABABBABCABABBA with 1=A, 2=B, 3=C outputs:
why: The slide's trace: 9 codes for 14 characters.

q: In the slide example, what is code 6?
why: s=AB, c=B → output 4, add 6 = ABB.

q: The last dictionary entry made for ABABBABCABABBA is:
why: s=ABB, c=A → output 6, add 11 = ABBA; then A is output at EOF.

q: Slide ratio for 14 characters sent as 9 codes?
why: 14/9 = 1.56 (counting symbols, not bits).

q: LZW of BABAABAAA with 1=A, 2=B outputs:
why: Entries 3=BA, 4=AB, 5=BAA, 6=ABA, 7=AA; the final s = AA is output as 7.

q: Decoder state: s = AB, next code 5 is not yet in the dictionary. Entry = ?
why: Exception handler: entry = s + s[0] = AB + A.

q: Decode 1 2 3 5 with 1=A, 2=B:
why: A, B (3=AB), AB (4=BA), 5 missing → AB+A = ABA. Total ABABABA.

q: When does the LZW decoder's exception handler fire?
choices: A code arrives before the decoder made it
A code is larger than the max code length
The input contains a symbol not in the initial table
why: The decoder is one step behind; if the encoder uses a just-created code, the decoder lacks it.

q: In LZW decoding, the new entry added is:
choices: s + first character of the entry
The current entry on its own
s + the last character of the current entry
why: Algorithm 7.3: add s + entry[0].

q: An LZW dictionary starts with code length l0 = 9. Its initial size?
why: 2^l0 = 2^9 = 512; when full, l grows by 1.

q: Why does arithmetic coding usually beat Huffman?
choices: It is not limited to whole bits per symbol
It uses a fixed-length code for each symbol
It builds a dictionary of long strings
It throws away the inaudible information
why: Huffman uses integer-length codewords; arithmetic coding treats the whole message as one unit.

q: In arithmetic coding a message is represented by:
choices: A binary tree of symbol codewords
A list of indices into a string dictionary
A run count followed by a symbol
why: The interval starts as [0, 1) and narrows with each symbol.

q: The slide's encoder updates low first, then high = low + range·Range_high. What goes wrong?
choices: high uses the new low; both need the old
Nothing; this is the correct update order
range must be updated before low is
why: Compute both bounds from the old low (and old range); the worked table follows that rule.

q: CAEE$: after C then A, the interval is:
CAEE$: after C, A, E, the interval is:
Final interval for CAEE$?
Final range for CAEE$ (p = 0.2, 0.2, 0.3, 0.3, 0.1)?
why: The final range is the product of the probabilities: 0.2·0.2·0.3·0.3·0.1.

q: Codeword chosen for CAEE$?
why: 0.01010101₂ = 0.33203125, the shortest binary fraction inside [0.33184, 0.3322).

q: How many bits does the CAEE$ codeword use?
why: 0.01010101 has 8 fraction bits.

q: Procedure 7.2 sets the next bit to 1, then changes it back to 0 when:
choices: The value is still below low
why: Set a 1; if value > high, replace by 0; stop once value ≥ low.

q: Decoding 0.33203125: after outputting C [0.3, 0.5), the next value is:
Decoder: value 0.8359375 lies in E [0.55, 0.85). The next value?
Table A [0,.4) B [.4,.7) C [.7,.9) $ [.9,1). Interval after C then A?
Same table: decode the value 0.7545.
Two different numbers inside the final interval [low, high) are decoded. They give:
choices: An error for one of them
why: Any value in the final interval identifies the message; the codeword is just the shortest binary one.

q: Lossy compression gives:
choices: A close approximation, much higher ratio
An exact copy at a much higher ratio
An exact copy at a much lower ratio
A close approximation, at a lower ratio than lossless
why: The output is not identical, but the ratio is much higher than lossless.

q: A 3-bit uniform quantizer covers [−4, 4). Step size?
Data rate of 44.1 kHz, 16-bit stereo audio?
The slide says '84M per minute' for CD audio. 84M of what?
why: 1.4112 Mbit/s × 60 ≈ 84.7 Mbit; in bytes it's about 10.6 MB.

q: CD audio (1,411.2 kbit/s) coded as MP3 at 128 kbit/s. Compression ratio?
Which of these is a lossless audio format?
why: FLAC and Apple Lossless are lossless, at the cost of larger files.

q: MP3 and AAC are both based on:
why: Both are lossy and use the modified discrete cosine transform plus psychoacoustics.

q: The human ear is most sensitive between:
why: Intermediate frequencies, where the basilar membrane reacts most. The hearing range is 20 Hz–20 kHz.

q: Masking is:
choices: One sound reducing perception of another
Adding noise to cover up the quiet passages of a song
why: A strong sound makes nearby (in frequency or time) weaker sounds inaudible.

q: A loud sound hides quieter sounds just before and after it. This is:
why: Temporal masking acts in time; frequency masking acts on nearby frequencies.

q: About how much SNR does each added bit give?
why: Each bit doubles the levels → about 6 dB more SNR; 16 bits ≈ 96 dB.

q: Why does masking allow compression?
choices: Raising the masked noise floor saves bits
Masked bands are then coded losslessly
It removes the need for a filter bank
It doubles the effective sampling rate of the signal
why: Noise under the mask is inaudible; a higher noise floor means fewer bits.

q: Sampling frequencies supported by MPEG-1 audio?
why: Precision 16 bits; sampling 32/44.1/48 kHz.

q: MPEG-1 Layer III (MP3) bit-rate range and target?
Which layer is the dominant standard for DAB radio and DVB TV?
why: MP2, from MUSICAM, is a time-domain sub-band coder used in broadcasting.

q: How many sub-bands does the MPEG audio filter bank produce?
why: The filter bank divides the input into 32 equal-frequency sub-bands.

q: Which order matches the MPEG audio encoder?
choices: Filter bank, psychoacoustic model, bit allocation, bitstream
Psychoacoustic model, bitstream, filter bank, bit allocation
Bit allocation, filter bank, bitstream, psychoacoustic model
Filter bank, bitstream, bit allocation, psychoacoustic model
why: Split into sub-bands, find what is masked, allocate bits, pack the bitstream.

q: MPEG bit allocation computes MNR as:
why: Mask-to-noise ratio = signal-to-noise ratio − signal-to-mask ratio.

q: Each iteration, bits are given to the sub-band with:
why: Lowest MNR = most audible noise, so it needs bits most.

q: SNR = 18 dB, SMR = 12 dB. MNR?
why: MNR = SNR − SMR = 18 − 12.

q: Bands with SMR 12, 3, 20, 8 dB all start at 0 bits. Which band gets the first bit?
why: MNR = 0 − SMR: band 3 has the lowest MNR (−20).

q: Pre-echo is:
choices: Sound heard before it actually occurs
An echo added after every loud sound
Noise above 20 kHz that gets removed
A delay between the two stereo channels
why: A transform-coding artifact most noticeable on percussion like cymbals.

q: Which two artifacts appear at too-low bit-rates?
why: Compression artifacts named on the slide are ringing and pre-echo.

q: AAC was introduced in 1997 as:
why: Introduced as MPEG-2 Part 7, folded into MPEG-4 in 1999.

q: Which is an AAC improvement over MP3?
choices: Pure MDCT filter bank, 8–96 kHz rates
A fixed 128 kbps rate and 32 sub-bands
Lossless coding of all audio content
why: AAC adds more sampling rates, arbitrary bit-rates, variable frame length and a simpler pure-MDCT filter bank.

q: Which MPEG-4 coder targets speech at 6–24 kbps?
why: Code-excited linear prediction: 6–24 kbps at 8/16 kHz. Parametric is 2–6 kbps.

q: MP4 (MPEG-4 Part 14) is:
why: A wrapper holding video and audio streams plus metadata.
